content: The standard treatment for high-grade glioma (HGG) typically involves surgical intervention, which may include either a biopsy or resection, followed by radiotherapy with or without the addition of temozolomide. A novel approach to drug delivery involves implanting chemotherapy-impregnated wafers directly into the resection cavity. This method aims to deliver therapeutic agents locally while potentially minimizing systemic side effects. However, the efficacy of this approach and its role in standard care for HGG patients remain uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of chemotherapy wafers in patients diagnosed with HGG. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as other sources such as the Science Citation Index and the meta-Register of Controlled Trials. Reference lists of identified studies were reviewed, and hand searches of journals like the Journal of Neuro-Oncology and Neuro-Oncology were performed for the years 1999 to 2010, including conference abstracts. Additionally, neuro-oncologists, trial authors, and drug manufacturers were contacted to identify ongoing or unpublished trials. The study included patients of all ages with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of HGG, determined through intra-operative analysis during their first surgical resection. The therapy could be administered as primary treatment for newly diagnosed disease or as treatment for recurrent disease. The intervention under investigation was the insertion of chemotherapy wafers into the resection cavity. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the relevance of the search results and critically appraised the studies based on pre-specified guidelines. For primary disease, two RCTs were identified that evaluated the use of carmustine-impregnated wafers (Gliadel®) and included a total of 272 participants. The results demonstrated that Gliadel® wafers significantly improved survival compared to placebo wafers, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.65 (95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.48 to 0.86, P = 0.003). In contrast, for recurrent disease, only one RCT was identified, which enrolled 222 participants. This trial did not show a statistically significant survival benefit for Gliadel® compared to placebo, with an HR of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.62 to 1.10, P = 0.2). No suitable data were available for secondary outcome measures. Adverse events were not more frequent in either treatment group and were described qualitatively. The authors concluded that carmustine-impregnated wafers (Gliadel®) improve survival without increasing the incidence of adverse events when used as a primary therapy for HGG. However, there is no evidence to suggest a benefit for other outcome measures. In cases of recurrent disease, Gliadel® does not appear to provide any additional survival advantage.
